<!-- rule: core/laws.md -->
## Laws

Each line is a summary; the file in brackets (a rule file, or a design document
and the heading in it) states it in full. The backend and frontend Laws files
beside this one hold the Laws for one stack.

- a gap with a doc page is still a gap: a known defect, an unchecked promise or
  a path that only works "because nothing does X today" gets fixed, not written
  up; refusing valid input is not a fix; `Accepts` holds deliberate trade-offs
  only [`coding/root-cause.md`]
- model the invariant before choosing enforcement or concurrency; the domain,
  not a caller, decides what the invariant is
  [`invariants/invariant-enforcement.md`]
- callers never re-derive a server rule: a UI reads the read model's
  `availableActions`, capabilities or named flag; a second use case calls the
  same decision [`frontend/server-rules-stay-on-the-server.md`]
- do not hand-roll commodity infrastructure, protocols, or dev tooling when a
  suitable maintained framework, library, official SDK, or generated client
  exists; custom machinery carries the same burden of proof as a new dependency
  [`coding/use-libraries-before-building-machinery.md`]
- in TypeScript app code, Vue template expressions included, no type assertions
  or non-null assertions [`coding/type-safety-all-stacks.md`]
- no check-then-write as the final correctness mechanism, no coordination
  machinery for a race that is merely conceivable, no hand-rolled locks or
  outboxes, no blind retries, and no outbox unless atomic state-plus-message
  publication is the invariant [`invariants/concurrency-laws.md`]

A Law beats any spec or plan Decision: when a design and a Law conflict, the
design changes, and a Decision that breaks one is a defect, not a choice.
<!-- rule: core/frontend-laws.md -->
## Frontend Laws

Each line is a summary; the file in brackets (a rule file, or a design document
and the heading in it) states it in full. These Laws apply together with the
cross-stack Laws in the Laws file beside this one.

- the API is not the information architecture: UI language and ordering follow
  the user's journey and desired outcomes, not transport models, backend
  operations, configuration variants, or implementation sequence
  [`ui/core-law.md`]
- provide implementations, not projections: a page that needs more of a
  capability widens its port; it doesn't unpack it, repack it, or add getters
  to hand out pieces
  [`frontend/page-ports-and-adapters.md#provide-implementations-not-projections`]
- frontend composition happens only in Nuxt shells: `app.vue`, layouts, and
  pages provide capabilities/contexts with `provideX`; components and
  composables only inject them with `injectX`
  [`frontend/page-ports-and-adapters.md#nuxt-shells-as-composition-roots`]
<!-- rule: core/rule-strength.md -->
## Rule Strength

Every house doctrine statement belongs to one of four strengths:

- **Law** — protects correctness, ownership, or dependency direction; a
  violation is a bug. If valid context contradicts it, the statement was a
  default or the checker produced a false positive, not a waived law
- **Default** — the preferred greenfield choice; replace it when the local
  constraint clearly points elsewhere
- **Preference** — house consistency with no claim of architectural necessity
- **Tooling** — a current replaceable implementation choice

Mechanical checks may fail builds only for laws and mechanically provable
correctness constraints. Defaults should warn, preferences should inform, and
tooling rules should remain easy to update. Do not give a filename convention
the same authority as an atomicity or dependency rule.
<!-- rule: core/defaults.md -->
## Defaults

Each line is a summary; the file in brackets (a rule file, or a design document
and the heading in it) states it in full. The backend and frontend Defaults
files beside this one hold the Defaults for one stack.

- prefer explicit, honest boundaries [`coding/core-rule.md`]
- seams must be earned [`coding/seams.md`]
- keep things local and preserve ownership when they gain more consumers
  [`coding/local-before-shared.md`]
- use the narrowest owner and smallest mechanism that make an invariant true
  [`invariants/invariant-enforcement.md`]
- a lifecycle with several guarded actions gets one pure decider
  (`Refusal` / `Available`) that guards the use cases and feeds
  `availableActions`; the decider explains, the database enforces
  [`invariants/deciders.md`]
- generated code is an external contract representation; add an
  anti-corruption layer only when it adds semantic value
  [`coding/generated-code.md`]
- tests default to real behaviour over mock soup and mechanically enforce
  modular boundaries
  [`tests/core-principle.md`, `tests/default-bias.md`,
  `tests/what-to-test.md`]
<!-- rule: core/frontend-defaults.md -->
## Frontend Defaults

Each line is a summary; the file in brackets (a rule file, or a design document
and the heading in it) states it in full. These Defaults apply together with the
cross-stack Defaults in the Defaults file beside this one.

- ask users for decisions they understand; progressively disclose the mechanism
  needed to express each decision
  [`ui/ask-for-outcomes-not-mechanisms.md`,
  `ui/prefer-progressive-disclosure.md`]
- make defaults, consequences, and the resulting outcome visible
  [`ui/make-the-default-legible.md`,
  `ui/explain-consequences-not-system-events.md`, `ui/show-the-result.md`]
- accessibility, formatting, display, or validation the spec leaves open follows
  the GOV.UK Design System and style guide, unless the repo's UI skill decides it
  [`ui/when-the-detail-is-unspecified.md`]
- frontends are SPAs (`ssr: false` assumed) [`frontend/single-page-apps.md`]
<!-- rule: core/preferences.md -->
## Preferences

- tooling stays boring and explicit
- no type-tag suffixes in TS file names (`.port.ts`, `.service.ts`,
  `.use-case.ts`); dirs carry the role; `<feature>.module.ts` exempt
<!-- rule: coding/core-rule.md -->
## Core Rule

Prefer explicit, honest code over clever, magical, or abstraction-heavy code.

The job is to make:

- ownership obvious
- provenance obvious
- dependency direction obvious
<!-- rule: coding/coding-style.md -->
## Coding Style

Defaults unless the spec or a Law states a hard boundary:

- **Data transforms over object hierarchies** — prefer plain `type` (TS),
  `sealed record` (C#), object spread, and pure functions. Behavioral entities
  are correct when their methods protect lifecycle invariants; inheritance-heavy
  domain models are not. For the enforcement ladder and concurrency admission
  policy, read `invariants/invariant-enforcement.md` and `invariants/concurrency-review.md`.
- **Minimal dependencies** — every package must earn its place. The absence of a dependency is a feature, not a gap.
- **Let patterns prove themselves** — prefer duplication over premature extraction. Three similar lines beats a premature helper. Extract when the pattern is real, not when it first appears.
- **Readability over abstraction** — procedural scripts that read top-to-bottom beat clever composition. A reader should understand each line without holding the abstraction in their head.
- **No `process.env` directly** — use the validated config object. Add new env vars to the Zod schema (`src/config.ts` or equivalent). Ambient config access is untraceable.
- **No self-narrating comments** — do not add comments that restate what the code plainly says. A comment earns its place only by explaining WHY: a non-obvious constraint, a design decision, or a real gotcha. Stream-of-consciousness narration ("now loop over the items") and notes-to-self are noise. When in doubt, leave it out.
<!-- rule: coding/use-libraries-before-building-machinery.md -->
## Use Libraries Before Building Machinery

**Law:** do not hand-roll infrastructure, security protocols, wire clients,
serialization formats, schedulers, storage clients, authentication flows, dev
tooling (comparators, parsers for standard formats, test harnesses), or
other general-purpose machinery when a suitable maintained library, framework,
official SDK, or generated client already exists.

“Minimal dependencies” cuts both ways. A package must earn its place, but custom
machinery must also justify the permanent implementation, security, testing,
upgrade, and operational burden it creates. Avoiding one dependency is not a win
when it makes the application maintain a private, incomplete implementation of a
solved problem.

Before writing custom machinery:

1. Identify the established framework capability, official SDK, maintained
   library, or authoritative generated-client option.
2. Check whether it satisfies the actual correctness, security, licensing,
   deployment, observability, failure, and retry requirements.
3. Use it behind the owning module's honest application port when semantic
   translation or dependency inversion is required. Keep third-party types and
   exceptions at the Infrastructure edge.
4. Configure or disable library behaviour that conflicts with application
   invariants, especially hidden retries, transactions, caching, or background
   execution.
5. Hand-roll only when no suitable option exists or a concrete hard requirement
   cannot be met. Record the exact disqualifying constraint and test the custom
   surface as infrastructure, not as incidental helper code.

The application still owns its product rules, capability contracts, idempotency
semantics, transaction boundaries, failure interpretation, and orchestration.
The database or established library owns concurrency arbitration and atomic
persistence mechanics; `invariants/invariant-enforcement.md` and `invariants/concurrency-review.md` define that boundary.
The library owns commodity protocol and runtime mechanics. Do not fork an SDK's
job into application code, and do not wrap a library one-for-one merely to hide
that it is a dependency.

This law does not require a package for every small pure function. A
dependency is unsuitable when its scope, runtime cost, maintenance state, or
semantic mismatch outweighs the small and fully understood code it would
replace. The distinction is commodity machinery versus local product logic, not
large code versus small code.
<!-- rule: coding/seams.md -->
## Seams

Seams must be earned.

Introduce a seam only when there is real:

- variability
- runtime boundary
- ownership boundary
- testability need
- cross-module dependency concern

Do not introduce seams just because the pattern exists.

Fake abstractions are worse than direct code.
<!-- rule: coding/root-cause.md -->
## Root Cause

Fix root causes before adding shims.

Prefer fixing:

- the real boundary
- the real model
- the real config
- the real dependency direction

**Law:** a gap with a doc page is still a gap. Writing a problem down does not
resolve it. A decision record, an `INVARIANTS.md` `Accepts`, a changelog "known
issue", a README caveat or a code comment never stands in for a fix.

- A **gap** is something wrong, unenforced or unchecked that could be fixed: a
  promise nothing verifies, an entry point outside a guard, a false positive, a
  rule that holds only "because no caller does X today".
- A **trade-off** is a cost chosen over a working alternative, for a stated
  reason, such as one more indexed query per cache miss rather than building
  stampede protection. Only trade-offs go under `Accepts`.
- The test: would we welcome a change that removed it at no other cost? If yes,
  it is a gap.
- A doc may say a gap exists only while a tracked fix for it is open, and names
  that fix.
- What to do with one: fix it now when this work caused or promised it, or the fix is trivial; otherwise report it as new work, never as a decision or a note.
<!-- rule: coding/local-before-shared.md -->
## Local Before Shared

Keep things local until they are genuinely shared.

Promote something only when it has:

- more than one real consumer
- stable enough ownership
- clearer shared value than local duplication

Do not create shared dumping grounds.

Shared use does not erase ownership. A capability used by several consumers may
still belong to one feature or bounded context. Move code to a shared kernel
only when ownership is genuinely shared; otherwise expose a public contract or
keep the implementation with its owner.
<!-- rule: coding/provenance.md -->
## Provenance

Names and file boundaries should reveal what a thing really is.

Prefer:

- capability names
- concrete implementation names
- direct imports from the real owner
- explicit registration and wiring

Avoid:

- vague names like `manager`, `helper`, `service`, `provider`
- wrapper layers that hide the real dependency
- re-export structures that hide provenance
<!-- rule: coding/typescript-defaults.md -->
## TypeScript Defaults

Treat TypeScript as a design tool.

Defaults:

- prefer `const` functions
- strict typing
- explicit state modelling
- fix the type or the code, not the symptom

Avoid:

- `any` as convenience
- type assertions and non-null assertions (a law; see `coding/type-safety-all-stacks.md`)
- optional-chaining away modelling problems
- nullish-coalescing away unclear state

Where runtime DI identity is needed, prefer abstract-class tokens with interface-like shape.
<!-- rule: coding/type-safety-all-stacks.md -->
## Type Safety (All Stacks)

No `object`, `object?`, `dynamic`, `any`, or `unknown` as value carriers. Model the actual type.

If a value can be string, bool, or number — make a discriminated union, not `object?`.

`Dictionary` / `Record<string, unknown>` only for truly dynamic data — user-provided key-value pairs, JSON blobs from external APIs, config maps with unknown keys. If the keys are known at compile time, use a record or named type instead.

Always prefer stronger typing over flexibility. If a design choice introduces `object?` or untyped dictionaries, that is a signal to model better, not to weaken the type.

**Law:** in TypeScript app code, Vue template expressions included, no type
assertion (`x as T`, `<T>x`) or non-null assertion (`x!`) quiets the compiler.
Fix the type at its source: a typed template ref, `v-model`, a type guard, or a
better model. `as const` and `satisfies` are fine; they check a type rather than
override it.
<!-- rule: coding/furniture-dependencies.md -->
## Furniture Dependencies

A small blessed set of libraries is **furniture** — stable, boring dependencies
whose value outweighs repeatedly rebuilding them. Furniture is permission to use
a proven implementation after its capability is justified, not permission to
introduce the capability without a requirement.

- Zod is TypeScript furniture at untrusted runtime boundaries.
- FluentResults is Application furniture in .NET, not Domain furniture; closed
  domain decisions should use domain-specific outcomes.
- `pg-advisory-lock` is TypeScript/PostgreSQL furniture for justified
  session-level advisory coordination.
- `DistributedLock` is .NET furniture for justified distributed
  synchronisation; use the provider for the system's existing authoritative
  store.
- Brighter is .NET furniture for justified durable messaging, service
  activation, inbox/outbox, and transport. It is not the default in-process
  mediator.

`invariants/concurrency-review.md` owns the admission rules, and `invariants/established-furniture.md` the
failure-model qualifications, for concurrency and messaging furniture. The
furniture list grows only by explicit ruling, never by precedent creep.
<!-- rule: coding/generated-code.md -->
## Generated Code

Generated code is already an external contract representation, but not
necessarily the capability boundary the application wants.

Do not wrap generated clients/contracts one-for-one unless there is real capability abstraction to add.

Good reasons to add a layer:

- combine multiple generated calls into one capability
- add non-trivial policy/orchestration
- hide a genuinely unstable external boundary

Bad reasons:

- “we always wrap APIs”
- renaming generated methods without adding meaning

Wrap generated code when ownership, semantic translation, volatility, or
testing requires an anti-corruption layer. Do not wrap it merely because it is
generated.
<!-- rule: coding/composition.md -->
## Composition

Prefer composition at the edge.

That means:

- `app.vue`, layouts, and pages compose frontend capabilities; local component
  collaboration uses props/events
- modules compose backend capabilities
- wiring is explicit
- assembly happens where ownership is clear

Avoid ambient dependency soup.
<!-- rule: coding/anti-magic-bias.md -->
## Anti-Magic Bias

Prefer explicit registration and orchestration over framework magic.

Be suspicious of:

- auto-scanning
- hidden container behaviour
- reflection-heavy conventions
- smart wrappers that hide where work really happens
<!-- rule: coding/review-discipline.md -->
## Review Discipline

When reviewing a diff or change:

1. **Enum/value completeness tracing.** When adding a new enum value, status, or type constant — trace every consumer (switch/case, filter arrays, display logic, serialisation). Verify the new value is handled everywhere. Pure diff review is not enough — read outside the diff.

2. **Two-pass priority.** Data safety and race conditions first (TOCTOU, check-then-write without atomic WHERE, find-or-create without unique index). Style and consistency second. Do not interleave severities.

3. **Fix-first heuristic.** When the review is also asked to fix: mechanical fixes (dead code, stale comments, missing includes, unused variables) are just fixed, without asking. In a read-only review, list them as mechanical. Ambiguous fixes (security, design decisions, removing functionality, >20 lines) are batched into one question with recommendations.

4. A documented gap is a finding. A known gap excused in a doc, `Accepts`, changelog or comment must be fixed, as if the doc did not exist (see `coding/root-cause.md`). Never resolve a finding by documenting it: a fix round that only rewords the doc to describe the defect accurately has not fixed it.

5. **Suppress noise.** Do not flag: harmless redundancy that aids readability, threshold values tuned empirically, assertions that could theoretically be tighter but already cover the behaviour.
<!-- rule: coding/smell-checks.md -->
## Smell Checks

The code is probably drifting if:

- provenance is hard to trace
- generated code is wrapped for sport
- tiny features are buried under heavy ceremony
- real complexity is hidden behind bland names
- the fix is local but the cause is systemic
<!-- rule: invariants/invariant-enforcement.md -->
## Invariant Enforcement

The governing sequence is:

1. State the invariant independently of implementation.
2. Put enforcement at the narrowest owner with enough information.
3. Consider concurrency only when a concrete interleaving can violate it.
4. Use the smallest established mechanism that keeps it true.
5. Prove the interleaving at the real arbitration boundary.

Do not let concurrency machinery become a substitute for modelling the rule.

**Law:** important product invariants are established by the domain and encoded
at an authoritative enforcement boundary. An LLM, controller, UI, prompt,
comment, or test suite is not the authority that decides what the invariant is.

Use the narrowest owner with enough information to enforce the invariant. An
abstraction earns its place when it shrinks the representable state space,
centralises a legal transition, or owns a real consistency boundary.

Choose by the kind of invalid state:

### Representation or local value

Prefer the smallest sufficient boundary:

1. a precise static type or discriminated union
2. runtime schema validation at an untrusted boundary
3. a parser or value object when raw construction must be prevented

Do not wrap every scalar. A parser or value object earns its place when it makes
invalid construction impossible or removes duplicated validation.

### Local business decision

Prefer:

1. a pure domain function for a decision over supplied state
2. a behavioural entity when methods must protect one lifecycle
3. an aggregate only when several facts form one atomic consistency boundary

Several fields participating in validation do not by themselves justify an
aggregate. Plain data and pure functions remain the default.

A lifecycle with several guarded actions gets one pure decider: `invariants/deciders.md`.

### Persisted relational state

Prefer:

1. database constraints for declarative truths
2. one atomic conditional SQL operation for state-dependent writes
3. optimistic concurrency when writers must detect stale state
4. a short transaction when one invariant requires several writes atomically

Application checks may improve errors, but the final authority remains the
constraint, conditional write, concurrency token, or transaction.

### Cross-process state

Cross this boundary only when the invariant actually does:

- use an established durable queue when the domain can assign serial ownership
  of work to a partition or consumer
- use an established transactional outbox when a committed database change must
  reliably produce a message
- use a durable workflow when the invariant spans non-transactional external
  systems and requires retries, compensation, or reconciliation

A queue changes ownership and processing topology. An outbox solves atomic
state-plus-message publication. Neither is a generic higher rung of database
concurrency control.
<!-- rule: invariants/deciders.md -->
## Deciders

**Default:** give an entity one decider, a pure module that answers "may this
action happen now, and if not, why?", when all four hold:

1. its lifecycle is a small closed set of states (an enum, or a few flags and
   dates that combine into one);
2. several user actions depend on that state;
3. the answer is needed in several use cases and on the page;
4. the decision is pure: facts that need I/O (in use, ready, anything left) are
   loaded first and passed in.

Fit is structural. A live bug, or a page that disagrees with the server, shows
where a decider would have helped; it is not evidence that one fits.

```csharp
public enum RecordAction { Amend, Extend, Suspend, Reinstate, Revoke, Surrender }
public enum RecordRefusal { Anonymised, Lapsed, Ended, AlreadyThere }

public static class RecordLifecycle
{
    public static RecordRefusal? Refusal(RecordState record, RecordAction action, DateOnly today);

    public static IReadOnlyList<RecordAction> Available(RecordState record, DateOnly today) =>
        Enum.GetValues<RecordAction>().Where(a => Refusal(record, a, today) is null).ToList();
}
```

- Inputs are plain state and the time, passed in. No I/O, no clock, no
  repositories, no services. A date-based rule takes the business date ("today"
  in the organisation's time zone) from the one clock every caller uses, not a
  UTC date cut from `now`.
- The refusal is a closed domain value, not an exception. The use case maps it
  once to the declared failure (`backend/results-vs-exceptions.md`).
- Every use case for those actions guards with `Refusal`. The read side projects
  `Available` as `availableActions` on the entity's detail read model, so no
  caller re-derives the rule.
- Formalise the decision only. The state change stays a plain transform (`with`,
  spread) in the use case unless the transform is itself a rule.
- The decider explains; the database enforces. It sits in front of, and never
  replaces, the constraint, conditional write, concurrency token or transaction
  that arbitrates races
  (`invariants/invariant-enforcement.md#persisted-relational-state`). A rule
  SQL must also express, such as a list filter by derived status, keeps its SQL
  copy, held to the decider by a test.

A policy is any pure decision. A decider is the policy that guards one
lifecycle's actions and lists which are open. Use a plain policy function when
there is one decision with one or two callers and no action list to show.

When a criterion fails, use the smaller tool:

- one action, guarded in one place: an inline guard, plus a flag if the page
  needs it;
- users need one yes/no about the entity, not an action list: project a flag on
  the read model;
- the system, not a user, drives the transitions (deliveries, deadlines,
  retries): conditional writes and constraints own them;
- an external system owns the lifecycle: mirror its states as a closed type;
- the database already expresses the whole rule: leave it there.
<!-- rule: invariants/concurrency-review.md -->
## Concurrency Review

**Default:** do not add infrastructure merely because a race is theoretically
possible. First state the invariant and show a concrete interleaving that would
violate it.

For a demonstrated race, prefer in order, this ladder:

1. explicitly accept last-writer-wins when it violates no invariant
2. database constraints
3. one atomic conditional SQL statement such as `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` or
   `UPDATE ... WHERE ... RETURNING`
4. optimistic concurrency through a version or concurrency token
5. a short database transaction at the appropriate isolation level
6. row-level locking when one decision genuinely spans existing rows
7. an established advisory or distributed-lock library when no database row,
   constraint, or atomic operation can represent the coordination target

Do not use a preceding existence check as the correctness mechanism for a later
write. `Exists` followed by insert or update is still a race; let the write's
constraint or predicate arbitrate it.

An advisory lock is not the default implementation of idempotency or duplicate
suppression. Use one only when the lock target is a real domain identity that the
earlier rungs cannot represent. Lock names, scope, timeout, cancellation,
connection loss, and release semantics are part of the design.

The application owns the meaning of an idempotency key, its scope, fingerprint,
replay policy, and expiry. The database or established library owns reservation,
concurrency arbitration, and atomic persistence. Idempotency is not content
duplicate suppression.
<!-- rule: invariants/concurrency-laws.md -->
## Concurrency Laws

- Never use check-then-write as the final correctness mechanism.
- Never add coordination infrastructure because a race is merely conceivable.
- Never hand-roll distributed locks, leases, heartbeats, fencing, outboxes,
  inboxes, retry schedulers, or durable queues unless explicitly required and no
  maintained framework or library satisfies the invariant.
- Never claim atomicity across a database and an HTTP API by extending a local
  transaction or holding a lock longer.
- Never use an outbox unless atomic state-plus-message publication is the actual
  invariant.
- Never retry a non-idempotent operation blindly.
- Never use an aggregate merely because several fields participate in validation.
- Never copy a domain decision into a caller. A second use case calls the
  decision; a UI reads its projection (a flag or `availableActions`).

If supposedly separate modules repeatedly require atomic changes to both models,
revisit the module boundary before adding coordination machinery.
<!-- rule: invariants/established-furniture.md -->
## Established Furniture

Furniture is available only after the `invariants/concurrency-review.md` ladder justifies its category:

- TypeScript with PostgreSQL session-level advisory coordination:
  [`pg-advisory-lock`](https://github.com/IlyaSemenov/pg-advisory-lock). It does
  not provide fencing or exactly-once execution; connection loss can release the
  lock while the callback continues. It requires a direct connection or
  session-pooled PgBouncer, not transaction or statement pooling.
- .NET distributed synchronisation:
  [`DistributedLock`](https://github.com/madelson/DistributedLock), selecting
  the provider package for the existing authoritative store and accounting for
  that provider's handle-loss and abandonment semantics.
- .NET durable messaging, service activation, inbox/outbox, and transport:
  [Brighter](https://github.com/BrighterCommand/Brighter), when the application
  genuinely needs those capabilities. It is not the default in-process mediator.

Where applicable, these libraries remove the justification for a private version
of the capability they provide. They do not remove the need to prove the
invariant, choose the correct boundary, or understand each provider's failure
model.
<!-- rule: backend/results-vs-exceptions.md -->
## Results vs exceptions

Declared failures are results;
undeclared failures are exceptions. If the contract declares the failure
(`.Returns<ErrorResponse>(4xx)`), the use case returns it as a value and the
endpoint maps it — declared failures are control flow the caller must handle,
and values make that visible. Exceptions are reserved for "this should never
happen" and are translated once by the error middleware. Do not throw for
outcomes the API contract promises; do not return result objects for genuine
programmer errors.

FluentResults (`Result` / `Result<T>`) is the default Application result carrier
when a use case has a small open set of ordinary failures. It is not Domain
furniture. Domain decisions with a closed set of meaningful outcomes should
return domain-specific result records or sealed outcome types so callers can
handle them explicitly. Do not hand-roll a generic Result library per repo.

A decider's refusal (`invariants/invariant-enforcement.md`, `invariants/deciders.md`)
is such a closed domain outcome. Each decider has one mapping from refusal to
declared failure, which owns the error codes and wording, and every use case goes
through it. Do not construct the failure for a refusal at the call site.

Authorization follows the same split. The endpoint applies the authentication
requirement and the named authorization policy unconditionally (`[Authorize]`,
`.RequireAuthorization()`, or a fallback policy); a decision that needs the
resource or its state is made in the use case, never in a controller.
<!-- rule: backend/typescript-style.md -->
## TypeScript style

- strict typing
- narrow ports as abstract classes with private constructors
- concrete adapters `implement` ports
- prefer constructor property promotion for injected dependencies
- explicit provider wiring
- no hidden framework abstraction layers

Example:

```ts
export class TickPet {
  public static inject = [
    "clock",
    "getWindowTitle",
    "petEffects",
    "petStateMachine",
    "petStatePersistence",
  ] as const;

  public constructor(
    private readonly clock: Clock,
    private readonly getWindowTitle: () => string | null,
    private readonly petEffects: PetEffects,
    private readonly petStateMachine: PetStateMachine,
    private readonly petStatePersistence: PetStatePersistence,
  ) {}

  public async execute(input: TickPetInput): Promise<PetState> {
    // ...
  }
}
```

Prefer:

- `public static inject = [...] as const` for `typed-inject`-assembled classes
- constructor property promotion for long-lived injected dependencies
- `private readonly` by default
- `protected readonly` only when there is a real inheritance reason

Avoid:

- constructor args assigned manually to fields for no reason
- grabbing dependencies from service locators inside methods
- mutable injected dependency fields
- barrel-heavy indirection that hides provenance
- framework or transport details in domain/application

Production source reads environment only in root configuration/bootstrap owners:
`config.ts`, `config.mts`, `config.cts`, `config/**`, `bootstrap.ts`,
`bootstrap.mts`, `bootstrap.cts`, or `bootstrap/**`, each optionally under
`src/`. In a workspace monorepo, each package root (directory with its own
`package.json`) is treated as a project root for owner matching — so
`server/src/config.ts` is an owner just as `src/config.ts` is in a
single-package repo. Module-local folders with those names are not owners.
Build-tool config files (`vite.config.ts`, `nuxt.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`,
etc. — any `*.config.{ts,mts,cts}` at a package root) are build-time tooling,
not production runtime source. Outside those roots, do not read `process.env`,
`globalThis.process.env`, `Bun.env`, `Deno.env`, or import named `env` from
`process`/`node:process`; inject the validated config object.
<!-- rule: frontend/page-ports-and-adapters.md -->
## Page-colocated Ports and Adapters

Use this when designing, reviewing, or refactoring a Vue/Nuxt frontend toward a
decoupled, page-colocated, ports-and-adapters shape with:

- dumb views/components
- page/layout/app composition roots
- pure logic separated from framework code
- explicit capability boundaries
- typed runtime wiring via provide/inject

This is the Meridian frontend default. Its sections are one design and are read
together: each assumes the others.

### Default Recommendation

Treat **`app.vue`, layouts, and pages** as the only composition roots.

This is deliberately stricter than generic provide/inject advice. Vue cannot
navigate from `injectX()` to the runtime provider. Restricting every `provideX()`
to three Nuxt shell locations makes the wiring searchable and predictable.

Do not default to:

- global stores for everything
- component-local business logic
- fake API service wrappers around generated clients
- `app/features/...` for code that is genuinely page-local

The stable boundary is the **page/layout-owned feature**, not the composable and
not the component.

### Core Principle

Keep views dumb and dependencies explicit.

The point of page-colocated ports and adapters is not “do DI on the frontend”.

The point is:

- rendering stays in views
- pure logic stays pure
- framework code stays at the edge
- capability wiring happens once in `app.vue`, a layout, or a page
- runtime seams are explicit instead of ambient

`provide` / `inject` is just the cleanest Vue mechanism for expressing that boundary.

### Dependency Rule

```text
logic/         ← pure TypeScript, zero Vue/Nuxt imports
ports/         ← typed capability contracts and provided-context contracts
adapters/      ← boundary implementations satisfying capability ports
composables/   ← framework-rich implementations / reactive contexts
app.vue/pages/layouts ← the only composition roots
components/    ← leaf views or explicitly named feature containers
```

Dependency direction is explicit rather than inferred solely from list order.

Meaning:

- `logic/` depends on nothing framework-specific
- `ports/` contain contracts and wiring helpers only; a framework-neutral
  capability port exposes plain values, while a provided Vue context may expose
  `Ref`/`ComputedRef`
- `adapters/` implement a port against generated clients, storage, or platform
  APIs; a pure adapter may depend only on `logic/` and `ports/`
- `composables/` may depend on `logic/`, `ports/`, generated Rivet clients, Pinia, VueUse, etc.
- only `app.vue`, layouts, and pages provide concrete capabilities or contexts
- leaf components render and emit; feature containers may consume composed
  contexts but never construct infrastructure

#### Cross-page feature shape

`app/features/<feature>/` is for a product capability spanning multiple
composition roots. It may contain `logic/`, `ports/`, `adapters/`, implementation
composables, and public types. A shell may import and construct that
implementation; the feature never provides itself.

Consumers import only the feature's deliberate public contracts and pure logic,
not its internal adapters. `app.vue`, layouts, and pages remain the composition
roots; a feature folder is an ownership boundary, not an ambient singleton or
automatic store.

### Standard Layout

Page-local code is colocated by default.

```text
app/pages/forms/
├── index.vue
├── [id].vue
├── components/
├── composables/
├── logic/
├── ports/
└── adapters/
```

For the root page, use an adjacent folder:

```text
app/pages/
├── index.vue
└── index/
    ├── components/
    ├── composables/
    ├── logic/
    ├── ports/
    └── adapters/
```

Do not promote code until its ownership and lifetime require it.

### Promotion

A page or layout subtree must not import another page's local implementation
directories. When code is needed by more than one subtree, preserve ownership:

- move a genuinely cross-cutting primitive to `app/shared/`
- move a cross-page product capability to `app/features/<feature>/`
- expose a feature-owned public contract rather than deep-importing its
  internals

`app/shared/` means no product feature owns the code. Multiple consumers alone
do not make that true. A promoted feature keeps its shape, and consumers import
only its public contract:

```text
app/features/auth/
├── ports/
│   └── auth.ts          ← the feature's port (type + provide/inject)
├── logic/
│   └── auth.ts          ← the feature's pure logic (e.g. getInitials)
└── index.ts             ← the public contract: exports Auth, injectAuth, provideAuth, getInitials
```

Rules:

- Promote only what is genuinely shared. The port type and provide/inject helper promote when the capability is wired at one composition root (e.g. layout) but consumed in another subtree (e.g. page components). Pure logic promotes when used by components in multiple page subtrees.
- Preserve feature ownership. Cross-page Auth or Recordings code belongs in
  `app/features/auth/` or `app/features/recordings/` when it remains a product
  capability. Use `app/shared/` for genuinely generic/co-owned primitives.
- No migration shims. Delete pass-through files left at old locations after
  moving code. A deliberate public feature entry point is specifically
  `app/features/<feature>/index.ts`; workspace package entry files named explicitly
  by `package.json#exports` and generated barrels are also valid. Other `index.ts`
  barrels are not public feature contracts by filename alone.
- Implementations stay with their owner. A root-local implementation stays
  beside its page/layout. A cross-page implementation may live in
  `app/features/<feature>/`, but only `app.vue`, a layout, or a page constructs
  and provides it.
- Delete the page-local file. When a port or logic module is promoted, remove the original — do not leave a re-export stub behind.

Example — Auth port promoted from page-local to the auth feature:

```text
Before (page-local only):
  app/pages/index/ports/auth.ts           ← owns Auth type + provide/inject
  app/pages/index/composables/useRivetAuth.ts
  app/pages/index/logic/auth-card.ts       ← owns getInitials

After (layout provides auth, sidebar + pages consume):
  app/features/auth/ports/auth.ts          ← promoted: Auth type + provide/inject
  app/features/auth/logic/auth.ts          ← promoted: getInitials
  app/features/auth/index.ts               ← the public contract
  app/layouts/default/composables/useRivetAuth.ts   ← stays: only layout calls it
  app/layouts/default.vue                  ← composition root: provideAuth(useRivetAuth())
```

```ts
// app/features/auth/ports/auth.ts — the promoted port
import type { Ref } from "vue";
import type { components } from "@<scope>/contracts";
import { useProvideInject } from "~/composables/useProvideInject";

type CurrentUserDto = components["schemas"]["CurrentUserDto"];

export interface Auth {
  currentSession: Ref<CurrentUserDto | null>;
  errorMessage: Ref<string | null>;
  isLoading: Ref<boolean>;
  load: () => Promise<void>;
}

export const [injectAuth, provideAuth] = useProvideInject<Auth>("Auth");
```

```ts
// app/layouts/default/composables/useRivetAuth.ts — composable stays at composition root
import type { Auth } from "~/features/auth";
// ...implementation...

// app/layouts/default.vue — composition root
import { provideAuth } from "~/features/auth";
import { useRivetAuth } from "./default/composables/useRivetAuth";

const auth = provideAuth(useRivetAuth());
```

```ts
// app/layouts/default/components/app-sidebar.vue — consumer imports the feature's public contract
import { injectAuth, getInitials } from "~/features/auth";

// app/pages/index/components/auth-card.vue — another consumer, same import
import { injectAuth, getInitials } from "~/features/auth";
```

### Logic

`logic/` is pure TypeScript.

Hard rule:

- no imports from `vue`
- no imports from `nuxt`
- no imports from `#imports`
- no framework packages

Put in `logic/`:

- pure transforms
- calculations
- derivation rules
- immutable data shaping
- domain-ish UI rules that do not require reactivity

If something can be a pure function, put it here.

Components may import `logic/` directly because it has zero framework dependencies.

### Ports

A capability port is a **narrow typed contract describing an operation the UI
needs from a boundary**. A provided context is a **reactive feature-facing
surface** made available to a Vue subtree. Both may use the same typed
provide/inject mechanism, but do not pretend a `Ref`-heavy view model is
framework-neutral.

If a dependency is local to one component relationship, it is not a port: pass
it as a prop and communicate upward with events. A provided port/context is
subtree-global by definition and therefore must be wired at a traceable Nuxt
shell.

Rules:

- one port per feature concern, not one port per function
- capability ports are operation-shaped, not DTO-shaped
- provided contexts are view-model-shaped and may expose reactive state plus
  user actions
- a port file holds only the port's type and its `[injectX, provideX]` pair from
  `useProvideInject` (Provide / Inject Pattern, below): it imports types and
  that helper, never `provide`, `inject`, or a value from `vue`, and declares
  nothing else
- ports are for capabilities the subtree depends on, not for disguising an existing client

Good:

- `Auth`
- `Recordings`
- `SubmissionStatusPort`
- `TimelineDisplayPort`

Bad:

- `CurrentUserDtoPort`
- `NotesApiPort` that just mirrors generated methods
- `FormDataService`

#### Naming

Use names that make runtime wiring obvious at the call site:

- injected capability consumers use `injectX`
- composition roots use `provideX`
- concrete implementation composables may keep `useX` when they are real Vue composables

Examples:

- `injectAuth` / `provideAuth`
- `injectRecordings` / `provideRecordings`
- `injectSubmissionStatus` / `provideSubmissionStatus`

Why:

- `injectX` makes it obvious that a component is consuming a provided port
- `useX` remains available for concrete composables such as `useRivetAuth` or `usePlatformAuth`
- components should generally import `injectX` from `ports/`, not implementation composables from `composables/`

### Provide / Inject Pattern

Use typed provide/inject helpers based on Vue `InjectionKey` and VueUse local injection.

This is the canonical frontend port pattern. The exported pair must be named
`injectX` first and `provideX` second:

```ts
export const [injectRecorder, provideRecorder] = useProvideInject<Recorder>("Recorder");
```

Do not export `useRecorder` for a provided port. `useX` names are for concrete implementation
composables or framework hooks. The distinction matters at call sites:

- `provideRecorder(usePlatformRecorder(...))` means the composition root is wiring the capability.
- `injectRecorder()` means the consumer depends on an already-wired capability.
- `usePlatformRecorder()` means the root is constructing a concrete implementation.

Canonical helper:

```ts
import { injectLocal, provideLocal } from "@vueuse/core";
import type { InjectionKey } from "vue";

export const useProvideInject = <T>(name: string) => {
  const key: InjectionKey<T> = Symbol(name);

  const useProvide = <U extends T>(value: U): U => {
    provideLocal(key, value);
    return value;
  };

  const useInject = (): T => {
    const value = injectLocal(key);
    if (value === undefined) {
      throw new Error(`[Context:${name}] inject() called outside provider`);
    }
    return value;
  };

  return [useInject, useProvide] as const;
};
```

The shape is structural, not just a search for `throw`: the returned tuple is
`[inject, provide]`; the inject function binds the result of `inject` or
`injectLocal`, tests the missing polarity (`undefined`, `null`, or a deliberate
falsy guard), throws on that branch, then returns that same binding as narrowed
`T`. A reversed guard that throws when the value is present is invalid.

Why this pattern:

- typed capability seam
- subtree-scoped dependency wiring
- no prop drilling
- no ambient global soup
- hard failure outside the composition root
- `provide*` preserves and returns the concrete implementation type so the composition
  root retains root-only orchestration capabilities while `inject*` consumers see only `T`

The provider is an identity function with a registration side effect. It must not
narrow its return to `T`: `U extends T` proves the implementation satisfies the
port, stores it under the narrow injection key, and returns the exact `U` supplied.
This does not weaken the consumer boundary because `inject*` still returns `T`.

This is runtime wiring, not the architecture itself.

### Adapters

Adapters are optional boundary implementations. They translate between a
capability port and HTTP, generated clients, storage, desktop APIs, or another
runtime. A pure adapter is the simplest form; an adapter may be constructed by
a composable when Vue lifecycle or reactivity owns its lifetime.

Rules:

- adapters should not contain presentation state
- pure adapters have zero Vue/Nuxt imports
- if construction needs `ref`, `watch`, or lifecycle hooks, keep that reactive
  shell in a composable and keep protocol translation in the adapter where it
  remains meaningful

Example:

```ts
import {
  createSection,
  removeSectionById,
  reorderSections,
} from "../logic/section-state";
import type { SectionStatePort } from "../ports/section-state";

export const sectionStateAdapter: SectionStatePort = {
  createSection,
  removeSection: removeSectionById,
  reorderSections,
};
```

```ts
// composables/useRivetAuth.ts
import { ref } from "vue";
import { client, type components } from "@<scope>/contracts";
import type { Auth } from "../ports/auth";

type CurrentUserDto = components["schemas"]["CurrentUserDto"];

export const useRivetAuth = () => {
  const currentSession = ref<CurrentUserDto | null>(null);
  const errorMessage = ref<string | null>(null);
  const isLoading = ref(false);

  const load = async (): Promise<void> => {
    isLoading.value = true;
    errorMessage.value = null;

    try {
      const result = await client.GET("/api/session");

      if (result.error === undefined) {
        currentSession.value = result.data;
        return;
      }

      errorMessage.value = "Unable to load the auth session.";
    } catch {
      errorMessage.value = "Unable to load the auth session.";
    } finally {
      isLoading.value = false;
    }
  };

  const implementation = {
    currentSession,
    errorMessage,
    isLoading,
    load,
    clearLocalSession: () => {
      currentSession.value = null;
      errorMessage.value = null;
    },
  };

  implementation satisfies Auth;
  return implementation;
};
```

```ts
// page composition root
import { provideAuth } from "./ports/auth";
import { useRivetAuth } from "./composables/useRivetAuth";

const auth = provideAuth(useRivetAuth());
auth.clearLocalSession(); // Available to the composition root.
```

```ts
// descendant component or composable
const injected = injectAuth();
injected.clearLocalSession(); // Type error: not part of Auth.
```

This composable-direct path is often the better default on the frontend.
Validate a named implementation with `implementation satisfies Auth` rather
than adding a `(): Auth` return annotation when it has capabilities needed only
by the composition root. The former checks port compliance without erasing the
richer inferred implementation type or applying excess-property checks to an
object literal.

### Provide implementations, not projections

**Law:** A composition root should not unpack a composable and manually repack selected
members into a port-shaped object. Pass the implementation directly to `provideX`;
the preserved concrete return type lets the root retain persistence and orchestration
capabilities while injected consumers receive only the narrow port. A page that needs more of a capability widens its port; it doesn't unpack it, repack it, or add getters to hand out pieces.

```ts
// Wrong: the page has become a hand-written adapter.
const effects = useFormEffects();

provideFieldEffects({
  effects: effects.effects,
  fields: sections.allFields,
  connectors: discovery.connectors,
  add: effects.add,
  remove: effects.removeEffect,
});

// Right: provide the owned implementation directly.
const effects = provideFieldEffects(useFormEffects());
```

This keeps pages as wiring shells rather than dependency assemblers. If direct
provision is impossible because a page must gather and forward state from several
unrelated composables, treat that as evidence that ownership is unclear, the port
republishes capabilities it does not own, or a dependent composable should inject
those capabilities itself.

Do not merely move that page-level assembly into a
`useFoo({ dependencyA, dependencyB, ... })` options bag. Runtime collaborators
should normally be obtained through their typed injected capabilities; constructor
arguments are reserved for identity and genuine per-instance configuration.

### Composables

Composables are the framework-rich layer.

They may own:

- `ref` / `reactive` / `computed` / `watch`
- VueUse
- Pinia when appropriate
- generated Rivet client calls
- side effects
- loading flags
- local UI orchestration

Composables should:

- inject a port with `injectX` when they depend on a provided capability
- keep pure logic out of themselves where feasible
- expose a clean capability-shaped surface

Composables should not:

- grow into god-objects
- hide large amounts of pure business logic

If a composable gets too large, pull pure logic down into `logic/`.

### Two Valid Implementation Styles

Both are valid. Choose the simpler one that keeps boundaries honest.

#### 1. Pure adapter + thin composable

Use this when there is real pure logic worth separating.

Pattern:

- page provides adapter
- composable injects port via `injectX`
- composable holds reactive state and delegates logic to the port

#### 2. Composable directly implements the port

Use this when the implementation is already inherently reactive/stateful and an adapter would just add ceremony.

Pattern:

- composable returns the port-shaped capability
- page provides that composable result directly

This is valid:

```ts
provideAuth(useRivetAuth());
```

Do not create an adapter just to satisfy a pattern if the composable is already the cleanest implementation.

### Nuxt Shells As Composition Roots

Compose capabilities only in:

- `app.vue` for application-wide lifetime
- layouts for shell/session lifetime spanning pages
- pages for route lifetime

Components and composables never call `provideX`. Local component dependencies
use props/events. This is a traceability law, not a preference. Test harnesses
(`*.spec.ts`, `*.test.ts`, `__tests__/**`, and a `tests/`, `test/` or `e2e/` tree
at the root of the frontend or of its package) may call `provideX` to stand in for the shell.

Composition roots may:

- create implementation composables
- provide ports
- compose presentational components

Composition roots should not:

- become a dump for business logic
- reimplement pure transforms inline
- hide composition behind global setup unless it is genuinely app-wide

Example:

```ts
import { provideSectionState } from "../ports/section-state";
import { sectionStateAdapter } from "../adapters/section-state";

const sectionState = provideSectionState(sectionStateAdapter);
```

Or:

```ts
import { provideAuth } from "./index/ports/auth";
import { useRivetAuth } from "./index/composables/useRivetAuth";

const auth = provideAuth(useRivetAuth());
```

### Components

Leaf components are presentational. Feature-container components may consume
an already-provided context when that keeps orchestration out of leaves; name
and place them so their role is obvious.

They may:

- render data
- hold local UI interaction
- emit events
- consume already-provided capabilities
- import pure `logic/` helpers directly

They should not:

- call generated clients directly
- own workflow orchestration
- construct infrastructure dependencies
- reach around the page composition root

### Rivet Rules

Generated Rivet clients are already typed contracts.

Therefore:

- do not wrap Rivet behind ports by default
- do not create fake API service layers unless there is a genuine need
- bootstrap Rivet once at the app boundary
- call generated clients directly inside the composable that implements the capability when appropriate
- the generated client and its DTO types come from the contracts package: `rivet/client-package.md`

Good:

- `useRivetAuth()` calls generated session client
- `useSubmissionMessages()` calls generated messaging endpoints directly

Bad:

- `MessagesApiPort` that mirrors generated methods one-for-one
- “service” wrappers that only rename generated methods

### When Not To Use This Pattern

Do not force the full page-colocated ports-and-adapters structure when the feature is tiny.

Skip ceremony when:

- the component is purely presentational
- the composable is already small and clear
- there is no real capability boundary
- no subtree wiring is needed

If something is trivial, keep it trivial.

### Failure Modes

Watch for these:

- ports around everything
- fake API abstraction over generated clients
- adapters with Vue imports
- composables importing adapters directly when the port seam should be used
- global stores used as a default transport for unrelated concerns
- promoting code to shared/global before it is actually shared
- re-export shims (`export { X } from "..."`) left behind after promotion — consumers should import from the promoted location directly
- page-local code prematurely moved into `app/features/...`
- product-owned cross-page capabilities erased into generic `app/shared/`
- `can…` / `available…` helpers that compare server status strings, timestamps,
  counters, version lists or roles to decide what the user may do (see
  `frontend/server-rules-stay-on-the-server.md`)
<!-- rule: frontend/single-page-apps.md -->
## Single-Page Apps

Frontends are SPAs: assume `ssr: false` throughout. SSR idioms (hydration-aware
`useAsyncData` patterns, server components) are not house style, and nothing in
these rules should be read as ruling on them.
<!-- rule: frontend/server-rules-stay-on-the-server.md -->
## Server rules stay on the server

**Law:** the UI never re-derives a rule the server decides. Whether an action may
happen now, whether an entity is editable, whether a draft differs from what is
published: read the server's answer from the read model, as `availableActions`,
a capability set, or a named flag (`canPost`, `hasUnpublishedChanges`). If the
DTO lacks it, add it to the DTO. Do not work it out from status strings,
timestamps, counters, version lists or roles.

Roles are no exception. Which pages, tabs and buttons a user sees comes from
capabilities the server sends with the session, computed from the same named
policies its endpoints enforce, not from comparing the user's role.

A copy that agrees with the server today is still a copy. Agreement sets how
soon to remove it, not whether.

Server-owned ids are the same. A route, link, query value, request or
comparison takes the id from the DTO, never a hand-written literal such as
`"acme-crm"`. A table keyed on an id may map it only to presentation (labels,
colours, icons; see below).

The UI owns client state only: unsaved edits, requests in flight, and the
validity of input the server hasn't seen. Gate an action on the server's answer
*and* client state, never on a copy of the server's rule.

Checking unsaved input in the browser for fast feedback is client state, and
the server always checks again. The rule's inputs still come from the server:
limits and allowed choices travel on the DTO (as a `min`/`max` or an allowed
list), not as hand-copied constants or predicates. A bare constant that can't
travel on a DTO is held to the server's by a parity test.

Mapping a server value to a label, colour, icon or ordering is presentation and
belongs in `logic/`. The test: if the UI's copy were wrong, could the user
attempt something the server refuses, or miss something it allows? If so, it is
a rule, not presentation.
<!-- rule: frontend/composable-files.md -->
## Composable Files

### File naming

Composable files are camelCase, matching the exported function: `useAuth.ts`
exports `useAuth`. Older code may differ; fix it when you touch it.

### Framework state (`useState`)

Nuxt `useState()` is blessed — **behind composables only**. `useState(` may
appear only inside `composables/` files; the composable owns the key and exposes
a named capability:

```ts
// composables/useAppBooted.ts
export const useAppBooted = () => useState("app-booted", () => false);
```

Every other layer — components, pages, plugins, logic, adapters — consumes the
owning composable (`useAppBooted()`), never the string key. Two files sharing a
bare key is provenance-invisible coupling; the composable makes the owner
greppable. There is no `state/` directory: composables are the state home in
this taxonomy.
<!-- rule: frontend/testing-bias.md -->
## Testing Bias

Prefer:

- tests of pure `logic/`
- composable/page integration tests
- outcome-based behaviour tests

Avoid:

- mock-heavy tests that verify implementation detail only
- component tests that need large fake environment setup because boundaries were ignored
<!-- rule: ui/core-law.md -->
## Core Law

The API is not the information architecture.

UI structure, terminology, grouping, and ordering follow the user's journey and
desired outcomes. They do not follow:

- API call order
- DTO or database field order
- configuration object shape
- provider implementation boundaries
- technical mechanism variants
- the order in which the backend happens to validate or persist data

Backend structure may constrain what is possible. It does not determine how the
product explains it.
<!-- rule: ui/start-with-the-users-job.md -->
## Start With The User's Job

Before designing controls, state:

1. Who is doing this?
2. What outcome are they trying to achieve?
3. What decisions must they make?
4. Which decisions depend on earlier decisions?
5. What does the user need to see to trust the result?

Turn those answers into the page structure.

A setup flow should read as a coherent journey when its headings alone are read
from top to bottom.

Good:

1. Name this export
2. Choose where it should send files
3. Choose which data forms will provide
4. Decide where and how files should be saved
5. Review the resulting destination

Bad:

1. Create contract
2. Select handler
3. Resolve resource
4. Configure expressions
5. Set collision policy

The bad sequence describes the implementation. The good sequence describes the
user's task.
<!-- rule: ui/ask-for-outcomes-not-mechanisms.md -->
## Ask For Outcomes, Not Mechanisms

Controls should ask questions the user can answer from their domain knowledge.

Bad:

- Literal
- Input
- String template
- Collision policy
- Dynamic path expression

Good:

- Save every file in the same folder
- Choose the folder using form data
- Keep the uploaded filename
- Rename the file
- Do not overwrite an existing file

Technical variants are often multiple implementations of one user intention.
Collapse them behind that intention.

For example, these are implementation mechanisms:

- fixed value
- value from one field
- template containing multiple fields

They can usually become one user action:

> Specify a value using text and form fields.

The revealed editor can support plain text, one inserted field, or several
fields without requiring the user to classify their configuration first.
<!-- rule: ui/order-by-the-user-journey.md -->
## Order By The User Journey

Order decisions according to how users reason about the task:

1. Establish context.
2. Make the primary choice.
3. Configure only what that choice requires.
4. Handle exceptional behaviour.
5. Review the result.
6. Confirm or save.

Do not make users answer downstream questions before they have enough context.

Keep dependent controls adjacent to the choice that reveals them. Do not split
one conceptual decision across separate cards merely because separate
operations or models implement it.

A useful test is:

> Would the user describe these as separate decisions?

If not, they should not appear as separate steps.
<!-- rule: ui/prefer-progressive-disclosure.md -->
## Prefer Progressive Disclosure

The common path should be immediately understandable. Advanced capability
should appear only when selected or needed.

Example:

```text
Where should files be saved?

(o) At the top of the document library
( ) In a folder
```

Selecting `In a folder` reveals a folder builder. The initial screen does not
need separate choices for fixed folders, data-derived folders, and templates.

Progressive disclosure is not hiding necessary information. It is presenting
information at the point where it becomes relevant.

A dropdown whose only option is the default it already holds is not a choice:
hide it (keep it mounted, with `v-show`) so it appears once configuring another
feature gives it a second option. Where that default's outcome isn't obvious,
state it as text in the dropdown's place (see `ui/make-the-default-legible.md`). A
required choice with one candidate is picked for the user. A target picker
(which stage, which list, or which column) stays visible even with one
candidate, because it shows what the setting points at, and so does a lone
stale "(unavailable)" option, because it shows the setting is broken.

Do not:

- show every technical mode simultaneously
- display empty advanced editors by default
- make uncommon complexity compete visually with the recommended path
- disable an unexplained control and expect the user to infer its prerequisite
<!-- rule: ui/make-the-default-legible.md -->
## Make The Default Legible

A selected default must communicate its resulting behaviour.

Weak:

```text
(o) Library root
```

Better:

```text
(o) At the top of the Documents library
    Files will be saved directly in Documents.
```

Use recommended defaults where the product has a safe, common choice. Explain
why the default is suitable when the consequences are not obvious.

Defaults must be safe. A convenient default that silently overwrites data,
broadens access, or loses information is not a good default.
<!-- rule: ui/explain-consequences-not-system-events.md -->
## Explain Consequences, Not System Events

Labels should express what will happen to the user's work.

Weak:

- Stop with an error
- Replace
- Fail
- Use literal

Better:

- Do not overwrite the existing file
- Replace the existing file
- Keep the uploaded filename
- Use the same folder every time

Supporting text should explain material consequences:

```text
Do not overwrite the existing file
The export will fail and the existing SharePoint file will remain unchanged.
```

Do not use help text to paraphrase the label. Use it to answer the next question
the user is likely to have.
<!-- rule: ui/show-the-result.md -->
## Show The Result

Configuration interfaces should make the resulting outcome visible whenever the
user would otherwise need to mentally execute the rules.

Examples:

- final file path
- generated filename
- recipient summary
- permission effect
- schedule
- filter result
- mapped data preview

For a file destination:

```text
Example destination

Documents / Applications / ABC-123 / evidence.pdf
```

The preview should update as configuration changes and use representative sample
values. Clearly distinguish an example or preview from a live operation.

A preview closes the gap between configuring rules and understanding their
effect.
<!-- rule: ui/use-domain-language.md -->
## Use Domain Language

Prefer terminology users encounter in their work over terminology from the
implementation.

Use:

- form data
- uploaded file
- document library
- existing file
- service area
- case reference

Avoid unless the intended user genuinely uses them:

- payload
- expression
- handler
- literal
- interpolation
- configuration version
- resource identifier

Technical accuracy is necessary, but internal terminology is not inherently
more accurate for users.

When a precise technical term is unavoidable, introduce it through familiar
language rather than making the user decode it.
<!-- rule: ui/treat-disabled-states-as-explanations.md -->
## Treat Disabled States As Explanations

A disabled control must have an evident reason and a clear route to enabling it.

Prefer:

- hiding an irrelevant control until its prerequisite is selected
- showing the prerequisite beside the disabled control
- explaining the required action in direct language

Weak:

> Add a compatible input in step 3.

Better:

> To choose a folder from form data, first add a Text field under Data to export.

Use step numbers only as secondary navigation aids. Describe the actual action
because numbering changes and users think in tasks, not indices.
<!-- rule: ui/group-one-decision-at-a-time.md -->
## Group One Decision At A Time

A visual section should answer one user question.

Good section headings:

- Which file should be uploaded?
- Where should files be saved?
- How should files be named?
- What should happen if the file already exists?

Avoid grouping controls merely because their values occupy the same backend
object.

Related questions may share a card, but each question needs a clear label,
short explanation where necessary, and visible selected outcome.
<!-- rule: ui/when-the-detail-is-unspecified.md -->
## When The Detail Is Unspecified

Where the spec or design leaves accessibility, formatting, display, or
validation open (how a date or an amount is shown, what an error message says
and where it appears, how a required or optional field is marked, what a screen
reader announces), check what the GOV.UK Design System and the GOV.UK style
guide do before inventing a rule: find the matching component or pattern and
follow it. Name the pattern in the spec or the report. A repo's own UI skill
wins where it already decides the case.
<!-- rule: ui/review-method.md -->
## Review Method

When asked to "look at this UI", review it in this order:

1. State the user's job and intended outcome.
2. Read headings and labels as a journey.
3. Identify controls named after implementation mechanisms.
4. Identify sections ordered after API or data-model structure.
5. Merge mechanisms that express the same user intention.
6. Establish the safe common path and default.
7. Progressively disclose uncommon or advanced choices.
8. Rewrite labels around outcomes and consequences.
9. Add examples or previews where users otherwise simulate rules mentally.
10. Check prerequisites, disabled states, validation, and recovery instructions.
11. Check that the final review or summary matches what will actually happen.

Do not begin with visual polish. Correct the conceptual model and information
hierarchy first. Styling a mechanism-oriented interface does not make it
user-centred.
<!-- rule: ui/review-questions.md -->
## Review Questions

- Can the intended user understand every choice without knowing the API?
- Are we asking for a user decision or exposing a technical representation?
- Does the order match how the task is performed and understood?
- Are conceptually identical decisions presented consistently?
- Can multiple technical modes become one progressive editor?
- Is the recommended path obvious?
- Are destructive, security-sensitive, or failure consequences explicit?
- Can the user see an example of the resulting outcome?
- Does help text explain something useful rather than restating the label?
- Could a user return six months later and understand the configuration?

If the answer to any of these is no, treat it as a product-design problem, not a
copy-editing problem.
<!-- rule: ui/testing-bias.md -->
## Testing Bias

Prefer tests that verify:

- journey prerequisites and ordering
- the common path
- progressive disclosure
- visible outcomes and previews
- material consequences
- validation and recovery guidance

Avoid tests coupled to accidental control topology or implementation
terminology. Test what the user can accomplish and understand.
<!-- rule: tests/core-principle.md -->
## Core Principle

Test **behaviour and boundaries**, not incidental implementation detail.

The goal is:

- confidence through refactor-safe tests
- fast feedback on real regressions
- minimal mock soup
- explicit testing at the seams that matter
- tests as close to the metal as practical
<!-- rule: tests/default-bias.md -->
## Default Bias

Prefer:

- pure logic unit tests
- integration and lifecycle tests at real seams
- architecture tests where boundaries matter
- outcome-based assertions

Avoid:

- tests that mirror implementation line-by-line
- mock-heavy tests of internal call sequences
- giant setup for small behaviour
- tests that break every time code is rearranged

For LLM-authored code especially, the safest default is:

- think through the behaviour
- write the real thing
- test the actual behaviour

Do not default to building the test around mocks first.
<!-- rule: tests/what-to-test.md -->
## What To Test

### Pure logic

If code is pure, test it directly.

That includes:

- transforms
- calculations
- rules
- validators
- mapping logic

These should usually be the cheapest and most stable tests in the codebase.

### Application / use case behaviour

Test use cases and feature flows at the level where real behaviour becomes visible.

Focus on:

- inputs
- outputs
- state transitions
- important side effects

Do not over-specify internal call choreography unless that choreography is itself the behaviour.

### Architecture boundaries

If the codebase depends on strict module boundaries, enforce them in tests.

Typical examples:

- module A may consume module B only through a consumer-owned required port, a
  provider-owned published contract, or a deliberate shared kernel
- no dependency on another module's infrastructure
- no dependency on another module's internal application types

If the boundary matters enough to talk about repeatedly, it usually matters enough to test.

Every .NET project that owns a `Modules/` tree needs mechanical coverage through
one of: [`Meridian.Analyzers`](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb/tree/main/dotnet/Meridian.Analyzers),
architecture tests that actually execute ArchUnitNET/NetArchTest rules, or
CI/task/script automation that invokes [Plumb](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb).
An analyzer attached only to an unrelated project, a package with no execution,
or a declared architecture rule that is never checked does not cover the modular
project.

### Infrastructure

Test infrastructure directly when:

- the adapter is non-trivial
- the mapping is important
- failure handling matters
- the external contract is brittle

Do not wrap every trivial adapter in heavy bespoke tests just because it exists.
<!-- rule: tests/near-metal-rule.md -->
## Near-Metal Rule

Keep tests as close to the real runtime path as practical.

That usually means:

- prefer real wiring over mocked wiring
- prefer real feature flows over isolated call-sequence tests
- prefer lifecycle/integration tests over synthetic unit shells when the behaviour crosses a seam

The default question is:

- “Can this be tested through the real boundary instead?”

If yes, do that.
<!-- rule: tests/frontend-bias.md -->
## Frontend Bias

Prefer:

- direct tests of pure `logic/`
- composable tests where state/orchestration matters
- page-level integration tests where wiring matters
- user-visible outcome assertions

Avoid:

- mock-heavy component tests for internal details
- treating presentational components as the main testing surface
- mounting half the app just to test a pure rule that should have lived in `logic/`
<!-- rule: tests/mocks.md -->
## Mocks

Mocks are allowed, but they should isolate volatility, not replace the whole world.

Default stance:

- do not mock unless there is a concrete reason
- prefer the real dependency if it is cheap enough
- prefer a fake only when the real thing is too heavy, slow, unstable, or operationally awkward for the test

Good reasons to mock:

- non-deterministic external systems
- expensive boundaries
- unstable infrastructure
- rare failure cases

Good reasons to use a fake:

- storage or transport is too heavy for the test but the behavioural contract still matters
- a cheaper in-memory implementation can exercise the same capability honestly
- the real dependency would make the test operationally brittle

A fake covers behavior above the port; it does not cover the real adapter.
Where semantic drift is plausible, run the same behavioral contract tests
against the fake and every real adapter.

Bad reasons to mock or fake:

- avoiding proper seams
- testing internal call order instead of behaviour
- making tightly coupled code appear testable
- making the test easier to write at the cost of realism
<!-- rule: tests/test-doubles.md -->
## Test Doubles

The default double is a **hand-rolled fake**; a mocking
library (NSubstitute, `vi.mock`) stays legal at narrow seams — density is the
smell, not presence. A file built from many `Substitute.For<>` calls is mock
soup; one substitute at a genuinely volatile boundary is fine.

Conventions:

- doubles live in `TestSupport/{Module}/`; in a TypeScript test tree, a
  lowercase `support/` folder inside it (`tests/support/`, `test/support/`)
- naming vocabulary: `Fake*` (behavioral fake), `InMemory*` (in-memory
  implementation of a storage/transport port), `Inline*` (synchronous stand-in
  for an async dispatcher). Never `Mock*`/`Stub*` for hand-rolled doubles — the
  name should say what the double *is*, not that it is a double of some kind
- test classes build their subject through a private `CreateUseCase()` factory
- inject `TimeProvider` (or the `Clock` port) rather than reading time ambiently

A stand-in API response (a Playwright `route.fulfill` body, a mocked client
result) is typed against the generated contract, with
`satisfies components["schemas"]["…"]` or a typed fixture helper, so a contract
change breaks the test at compile time instead of leaving it to drift.
<!-- rule: tests/test-substrate.md -->
## Test Substrate

Integration tests run on the production database engine. `UseInMemoryDatabase`
is banned anywhere in test source — the EF InMemory provider validates neither
SQL nor relational behavior (no FK enforcement, no real query translation), so it
manufactures confidence. SQLite is not a substitute for PostgreSQL-specific
SQL, collation, transaction, or concurrency behavior. Use Testcontainers. A
good fixture starts one PostgreSQL container for the whole run, migrates a
template database once, gives each test fixture its own database copied from
that template (`CREATE DATABASE … TEMPLATE …`), and resets data between tests
with [Respawn](https://github.com/jbogard/Respawn), so tests stay isolated
without paying for a container or a migration per fixture. The `tests/near-metal-rule.md` rule
applies: if the adapter behavior under test touches PostgreSQL, the test should
touch PostgreSQL.

If a test wants to avoid persistence entirely, the fake goes at the
**repository/query port**, never underneath the real adapter as a fake
database. Either the test exercises the real adapter against a real engine, or
it fakes the port and the adapter isn't under test at all — there is no honest
middle.

Tests themselves are exempt from production-code rules (layer purity, module shape,
.NET style):
test code can import whatever it needs; it is judged by the testing rules' standards
(double vocabulary, mock density, location), not by production-code rules.
<!-- rule: tests/test-location.md -->
## Test Location

Frontend tests live in a top-level `tests/` directory at
the frontend root, mirroring source structure — not colocated `__tests__/` dirs
and not specs scattered beside source files. A Playwright suite may instead sit
in a top-level `e2e/` beside it (Playwright's own suggested name). A TypeScript API or
library keeps its tests in a top-level `test/` or `tests/` directory at its package root.
Backend tests live in the conventionally named sibling test project (`*.Tests`).
<!-- rule: tests/coverage-honesty.md -->
## Coverage Honesty

A green suite that tests the wrong things proves nothing.

Every materially different outcome introduced by a change (e.g. the
404/422/success mapping of a new endpoint) needs evidence at the cheapest honest
level. Several implementation branches producing one behavior do not
necessarily need separate tests. Covering the assembler, wiring, or setup does
not cover the use case that calls it.

A test using a fake or mock can cover the subject's behavior, but it does not
cover the substituted adapter. State that scope honestly. Verifying only the
double's calls, rather than an observable result or state transition, usually
manufactures confidence.

A check that can't fail is a defect: compare a check's result with something the code under test didn't produce.
<!-- rule: tests/tests-state-intent.md -->
## Tests State Intent

A test asserts the behaviour the product intends, even when today's code fails
it. A test written to match a known gap hides the gap: when a test reaches one,
assert the correct behaviour, report the red step, and fix the gap if this work
caused it or the fix is trivial; otherwise park it as new work. If the gap is
parked rather than fixed in the work, mark the test as an expected failure that
names the park (Playwright's `test.fail()`, or the framework's equivalent; a skip
isn't one, because it asserts nothing), so the suite goes red the day the gap is
fixed and the mark comes off. Weakening the assertion instead shrinks the check to
make it pass, which is never allowed.

In an end-to-end run, a fake adapter's failure modes are reached through agreed
trigger values in the fake (a postcode that always means "no results", another
that means "look-up down"), not by intercepting the page's requests
(`page.route`), so the journey drives the real path to the failure.

Keep journeys simple and happy-path first, and make them resilient: role or
test-id selectors, no sleeps, and no state shared between tests.
<!-- rule: tests/suite-size.md -->
## Suite Size

Every test costs run time and upkeep, so each one earns its place by proving
behaviour nothing else proves, at the cheapest level that proves it (see `tests/risk-and-test-shape.md`). New behaviour gets a test; extend an existing test before
writing a new one. No tests for copy, styling, colour, or layout. A change that
makes a test redundant deletes it in the same change.
<!-- rule: tests/risk-and-test-shape.md -->
## Risk and Test Shape

Do not pursue one universal test pyramid or direct branch coverage quota. Match
the test to the failure risk:

- pure decision errors → focused unit tests
- application orchestration errors → behavior tests through ports
- persistence/protocol errors → real adapter integration tests
- wiring errors → host/page composition tests
- critical user journeys → a small number of end-to-end tests
<!-- rule: tests/smell-checks.md -->
## Smell Checks

A test strategy is probably wrong if:

- a small behaviour needs huge setup
- most assertions are about how code was called rather than what happened
- tests break whenever code is rearranged but behaviour is unchanged
