- boundaries are constantly discussed in reviews but never enforced in tests
- the test suite is mostly mocks with very little real behaviour exercised
- new decision branches or error paths have no direct test exercising them
<!-- rule: rivet/client-package.md -->
## Rivet Client Package

The contracts package is the workspace package UI apps import the generated
Rivet client and DTO types from. Its sections are one design and are read
together: each assumes the others.

### Generated Output

Generated Rivet output lives in a workspace package, `packages/contracts`,
consumed through its `exports` map (`@<scope>/contracts`, or a `./client`
subpath), never an in-app directory.

- generated code is read-only; exclude from lint
- regenerate via the repo's task convention (`task generate`, `pnpm rivet`, or `dotnet rivet --project ... --output ...`)
- commit regenerated output with the contract change that caused it
- `--verify` is the CI drift gate

Source of the standard facade: https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/rivet-ts/blob/main/src/infrastructure/codegen/client-package-emitter.ts

### TypeScript Client Package

The frontend contract package has:

- `generated/openapi.json` — OpenAPI 3.1 emitted from the authored Rivet contract
- `generated/schema.d.ts` — `openapi-typescript` output over that spec
- `src/index.ts` — the hand-owned client facade consumed by UI apps

Standard facade shape:

```ts
import createOpenApiClient, { type Client, type ClientOptions } from "openapi-fetch";
import type { paths } from "../generated/schema.js";

export type { components, paths } from "../generated/schema.js";

export type RivetFetch = (input: Request) => Promise<Response>;
export type RivetConfig = Omit<ClientOptions, "baseUrl" | "fetch"> & {
  readonly baseUrl?: string;
  readonly fetch?: RivetFetch;
};
export type RivetClient = Client<paths>;

export const createClient = (config: RivetConfig = {}): RivetClient =>
  createOpenApiClient<paths>(config);

export let client: RivetClient = createOpenApiClient<paths>();

export const configureRivet = (config: RivetConfig): void => {
  client = createClient(config);
};
```

Rules:
- UI imports `client`, `createClient`, `configureRivet`, and DTO types from the contracts package
- UI does not create `openapi-fetch` clients directly
- regeneration updates `generated/`; the facade is hand-owned after scaffold
- do not wrap the generated client one-for-one in a fake API service

### Frontend Result Handling

The current v2 client is an `openapi-fetch` facade. Capture its `{ data, error,
response }` result and inspect the error channel or response status explicitly:

```ts
const result = await client.GET("/api/mappings");
if (result.response.status === 404) return null;
if (result.error !== undefined) return { ok: false as const, error: result.error };
return { ok: true as const, data: result.data };
```

Do not narrow on `result.data` truthiness: valid payloads may be `false`, `0`,
an empty string, or null. `try/catch` is for transport/network failure only;
never use catch for HTTP status branching.

Legacy Rivet v1 clients use `{ unwrap: false }` plus `.isOk()` /
`.isNotFound()`. Do not copy that API into v2 code.
<!-- rule: tools/typescript-vue-nuxt.md -->
## TypeScript / Vue / Nuxt

### Default stack

- package manager: `pnpm`
- framework: `Nuxt 4` + `Vue 3`
- language: `TypeScript`
- typecheck: `vue-tsc`
- UI layer: `@nuxt/ui`
- utility layer: `@vueuse/core`
- validation/schema: `zod` when needed
- tests: `vitest` + `@vue/test-utils` + `happy-dom`
- e2e: `playwright` where warranted

### Dependency injection

For explicit runtime DI in TypeScript backends or local hosts:

- prefer `typed-inject`

Use it when:

- you want explicit composition without Nest-style framework DI
- you are bootstrapping a local API/runtime host
- you want typed assembly with obvious provenance

Do not use it to hide boundaries or to recreate a magic container culture.

### Linting and formatting

Default bias:

- prefer `oxlint` over `eslint`
- prefer `oxfmt` over Prettier
- use `eslint` only where Vue/Nuxt support is still needed

Current practical rule:

- `ox*` does the general JS/TS lint/format work
- `eslint` remains for Vue/Nuxt-specific linting because `oxlint` does not cover that fully yet

So the intended stack is:

- `oxlint`
- `oxfmt`
- `eslint` + `@nuxt/eslint` only as the Vue/Nuxt layer on top

**Base configs.** The base config files live in
[plumb's `configs/` folder](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb/tree/main/configs),
and Plumb enforces them (MER-TO-002/005): every TS repo carries
`.oxlintrc.json` and `.oxfmtrc.json` containing *at least* the base settings,
with the base values — repos extend the base (extra rules,
ignorePatterns, internalPattern aliases), never contradict it. Apps with `.vue`
files additionally carry the `@nuxt/eslint` layer; apps without `.vue` files
carry no eslint at all.

**Comment width (preference).** `oxfmt` does not wrap comments, so keep
comment-only lines within the `.oxfmtrc.json` `printWidth` by hand; a single
unbreakable token (URL, path) may overflow, and so may a tool directive
(`// eslint-disable-next-line … -- reason`, `// @ts-expect-error …`), which its
tool reads from that one line.

### Generated code

Generated output is read-only and must be excluded by every applicable linter.
Each generated tree is covered by the nearest `.oxlintrc.json`
`ignorePatterns`; when an ESLint flat config applies to that tree, its exported
config also includes a matching `ignores` entry.

### TS examples

Base configs (the enforced minimum):

- [oxlintrc.json](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb/blob/main/configs/oxlintrc.json)
- [oxfmtrc.json](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb/blob/main/configs/oxfmtrc.json)

Nuxt + `oxlint` + `eslint` integration:

```js
// apps/ui/eslint.config.mjs — eslint is only the Vue/Nuxt layer; oxlint does the rest.
// @nuxt/eslint writes ./.nuxt/eslint.config.mjs during `nuxt prepare`.
import withNuxt from "./.nuxt/eslint.config.mjs";

export default withNuxt({
  name: "project/vue-rules",
  rules: { "vue/multi-word-component-names": "off" },
}).append({ ignores: [".nuxt/**", ".output/**", "dist/**"] });
```

Typed DI / explicit assembly examples:

- [quotes.module.ts](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/rivet-ts/blob/main/templates/example/apps/api/src/modules/quotes/quotes.module.ts):
  the module owns its `createInjector()` wiring; the root supplies only the
  adapters that differ between environments
- [list-quotes.ts](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/rivet-ts/blob/main/templates/example/apps/api/src/modules/quotes/application/list-quotes.ts):
  a use case with `static inject` and an abstract-class port
- [composition.ts](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/rivet-ts/blob/main/templates/example/apps/api/src/composition.ts):
  the composition root

Concrete `typed-inject` class shape: see `backend/typescript-style.md`.

### Notes

- Prettier is not the current default in newer repos.
- Older repos may still contain heavier ESLint/Prettier/plugin stacks; do not treat those as the preferred baseline.
<!-- rule: tools/workspace-orchestration.md -->
## Workspace / orchestration

When the repo is a real monorepo:

- package manager: `pnpm`
- task graph/caching: `turbo`

For local orchestration:

- use `Task` / `go-task`
- prefer `Taskfile.yml` over ad hoc shell sprawl once commands become real workflow
<!-- rule: tools/plumb.md -->
## Mechanical Checking

[Plumb](https://github.com/maxanstey-meridian/plumb) checks a repo against this
doctrine. Run it only when the repo's instructions name Plumb or the repo
defines a Plumb task or script; otherwise skip it, and don't report it as
unavailable. When it applies, run it after completing changes and fix all
error-level findings:

- if the repo defines a Plumb task or script (for example `task plumb`), run
  that: it applies the repo's own baseline and options;
- otherwise run it the way the repo's instructions say, or from a local
  checkout: `<plumb-checkout>/plumb . --json`.

If the repo uses Plumb but it won't run, say so in your report rather than
skipping the check silently. Setup is in its README.

Each finding's `docRef` (`rules/<folder>/<file>.md#<slug>`) names the rule file
or design document under the meridian skill's `references/` and the heading it
enforces; read that rule before fixing. Fix `error` findings unprompted. For
`warn` findings, fix them or state the exception that applies. Do not re-run
Plumb in a loop on a repo you have not changed.

Plumb's findings are the floor, not the review. A clean Plumb run is not a
review.
<!-- rule: tools/commits.md -->
## Commits

Commit messages follow Conventional Commits 1.0, and versions follow
Semantic Versioning derived from them. The message's job is to let a reader
of `git log --oneline` see what each commit did, and a reader of the full
message see what changed for the user and why.

The shape:

```
type(scope): subject

Body: what changed for the user, and why, in plain English.

BREAKING CHANGE: what a consumer must change.
```

- the subject is `type(scope): subject`: imperative mood, lower-case, no full
  stop, under 72 characters; it names the change, not the files
- the type is one of `feat` (new behaviour, a new rule, step, or capability),
  `fix` (a correction to behaviour or doctrine), `docs`, `refactor`, `test`,
  `build` (the build, dependencies, generated output), or `chore`
- the scope is the folder or module the change lives in, as the repo names it
  (`cycle`, `meridian`, `examples`, a feature folder in an app); there is no
  fixed list per repo, and a change across the whole repo has no scope
- a blank line, then the body: prose, wrapped at 72 columns, saying what
  changed for the user and why; the subject never carries the body
- a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for anything a consumer depends on: a renamed or
  removed rule file or heading (Plumb's docRefs resolve against them), a
  routine's arguments or report format, a repo's shortcuts in its
  instructions, a published package's API, a stored data shape
- one commit per reviewed unit: a `/cycle` round is one commit, typed by its
  highest-ranked change (breaking, then `feat`, then `fix`, then the rest),
  with the rest listed in the body; a round is never split by type after
  review, since that invents history

The version follows the commits since the last tag: a `BREAKING CHANGE`
bumps the major, a `feat` the minor, a `fix` the patch. Tagging is an action
only the user names.

Good:

```
refactor(meridian): merge each design's sections into one document

Each multi-part design is now one document, read whole, and every
bundle that carries part of a design carries all of it.

BREAKING CHANGE: rule files renamed and merged; docRefs move with them
```

Bad:

- a 500-character subject with no body
- `Review fixes: …` or `Update laws.md`: no type, and the subject names the
  activity or the file, not the change
- a subject copied from the repo's recent log: the log is the output of this
  rule, never its source
